title: Gasoline pushes US inflation to 3.7%
statLabel: US consumer prices, 12 months to September 2026 · BLS, Oct 14, 2026
body: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the past year, up from 3.4% in August. Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month and 34.2% over the year, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics says it accounted for over half of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3% in the month and 2.6% over the year, a bit above the 2.5% economists expected, with shelter, airfares and used cars doing the pushing. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.28% that morning as investors weighed whether the Fed raises rates again at its October 28 meeting.
why: Headline inflation tells you what your budget feels; core tells you what is likely to stick. Energy shocks can reverse, but if core keeps creeping up, borrowing costs stay high for longer, which matters for mortgages, business loans and the real return on cash. Check whether your savings rate is beating 3.7% before taxes.

sources.name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI release, Oct 14, 2026

title: A Chinese chip claim knocks 10% off SK hynix in a day
statLabel: SK hynix share price change on Oct 13, 2026, Korea JoongAng Daily
body: Over the weekend, the president of ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China's largest DRAM maker, said it plans to ship DDR5 server memory built on a new '4F²' cell design by the end of 2026. That layout packs memory cells into roughly 30% less space than today's mainstream design, which could make each bit cheaper to produce. Memory stocks fell on Monday, with Micron down about 4%, and on Tuesday in Seoul SK hynix closed down 10.09% and Samsung Electronics down 7.39%, while the Kospi briefly dropped below 6,000 and triggered a trading curb. Morningstar analysts said mass-producing the design reliably will be 'extremely difficult', and the shortage is still in place: TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise another 10–15% this quarter.
why: Memory chips are close to a commodity, so the biggest risk to today's record profits is new supply, not falling demand. Micron's adjusted gross margin hit 87% last quarter, up from 45.7% a year earlier, and markets now react sharply to any sign that a competitor could add capacity. If you own broad Korea, chip or AI funds, check how much of them sits in just three memory makers.

title: Oil tops $106 again, and diesel is the real squeeze
statLabel: US average diesel price per gallon, AAA · Oct 9, 2026
body: Brent crude rose to about $106 a barrel on Monday after Houthi strikes on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and two tankers were attacked near Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz, a route that carried about a fifth of global oil and LNG trade before the Iran war. Diesel is under even more pressure than crude: the US average is $6.28 a gallon, near the record $6.52 set on September 22, and the US diesel crack spread (diesel price minus crude price) passed $100 a barrel for the first time in August. Russian diesel output is down about 30% after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries, and US refineries ran at 98% of capacity in late August, the most since 2018. On October 9 the White House announced a deal for Russian diesel, starting with more than 300,000 tons, but analysts quoted by AP expect little effect on prices.
why: Diesel moves trucks, tractors, ships and generators, so its price shows up later in groceries, delivery fees and anything that has to be shipped. If your business moves goods, check whether your carriers add fuel surcharges and how fast they pass them on. Wednesday's September inflation report will show how much of this is already reaching consumer prices.

title: Long-term rates are above 5%, and mortgages followed
body: The Fed's target rate is 3.75–4.00% after a hike in September, with the effective rate at 3.88%. But the 10-year Treasury yield, which long-term loans follow, has climbed to 5.22%, and 30-year fixed mortgages average about 7.5%. Households now expect 3.9% inflation over the next year, the highest since May 2023, so lenders want more yield to lock money up for a decade.
why: Borrowing for a home or a business costs more, for longer. Cash and short-term Treasuries pay well right now, while long bonds swing with every inflation report. Watch the September inflation report on October 14 and the Fed decision on October 28.
